contributions.text_english:
I'm grateful to the Member for raising this very important issue, which, as I said earlier, has been an issue, sadly, since the beginning of the year, has at various times worsened, and we are going through a period of great concern, particularly in relation to the issue of diesel prices, as she suggests.

Fuel pricing is reserved to Westminster, and there's an important role for the UK Government here, and also the Competition and Markets Authority. I have raised the issue of fuel resilience, pricing and UK Government support with the UK energy Minister at a recent inter-ministerial meeting. I've called for appropriate UK Government support in situations where prices are escalating, and that remains our fundamental position.

We recognise the impact that road fuel price increases are having on household budgets, particularly, of course, when it's combined with the high cost of heating oil and the significant increases expected in the domestic energy price cap in January.

The Welsh Government recognises also that the sustained high fuel costs have consequences right across the Welsh economy. She mentioned the haulage sector and my colleague the Deputy Minister for Transport meets regularly with the haulage sector, has already discussed this issue earlier this year, and will continue to monitor the impact on that particular sector. It isn't, of course, limited to that sector. I'm conscious as well of the impact on bus operators, and I know that the Deputy Minister for Transport is meeting bus operators imminently, again to understand the particular problems that are arising now from the spike that the Member refers to.

Across the wider economy, of course, these increases, they raise operating costs, they raise distribution costs for all fuel-dependent sectors directly and indirectly. In all of our engagement, therefore, with the UK Government and other UK stakeholders, we will continue to raise these important matters, ensure that contingencies, where necessary, are put in place, and that the UK Government uses the full range of intervention tools and levers that they have—I'm particularly thinking now in the context of the budget—so that both businesses and hard-pressed households receive the support that is necessary at this difficult time.

I met with Valero recently in Pembroke to have a wide-ranging discussion with them. They are an important employer in that region, and, indeed, through the supply chain, to Wales as a whole. They are one of only four remaining refineries across the UK, and they represent a critically important bit of critical national infrastructure. If we were not previously aware of that, we've certainly been made aware of that by the geopolitical insecurity of the last nine months. I certainly will speak with them. I'm sure they have been in regular touch with the UK Government in terms of the contingency planning that I've referred to, and we engage with the UK Government on that front as well. But I certainly will want to know what the latest position is. Of course, it's a complicated situation there, where they are also an important exporter to the US, and, actually, there would be a knock-on effect to US oil supplies. There are complicated reasons as to why that historically is true. So, it certainly is an important area, where we will be engaging with the UK Government and with Valero.

In relation to the broader points that Janet Finch-Saunders made, I think it certainly is an important factor that there is geographic variation across the UK in terms of fuel prices. There is some limited recognition through the UK Government of that in certain areas, but not to rural areas of Wales. I think that now is an important time to revisit that question in terms of equity and to see not just what the UK Government could do in terms of fuel prices in general, where it does need to act at this particular time, but also to recognise the particular impact in rural communities, which face even higher fuel prices than the average. We will certainly take those points forward in our discussions with the UK Government as well.

I just would point out to the Member that I think the context is key here, isn't it?  So, the situation in Wales where we have unique assets—latent potential in many cases in terms of green energy—is that, actually, green energy is the means for our reindustrialisation, not our deindustrialisation. I'm specifically referring to, for example, our globally significant potential in terms of floating offshore wind, and the well-known, unique natural advantages we have in terms of tidal technologies, for example. We could, therefore, not just generate the electricity through those technologies, but also capture the supply chain and build up a manufacturing base on that level.

In relation to his point about nuclear, I would just point out that, actually, the move towards an emissions-based target includes not just renewable sectors, but also other low-carbon technologies that include nuclear, alongside carbon capture and storage.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Welsh Defence Ethical Framework
contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Llywydd. Today I'm updating Members on the Welsh Government's work to develop an ethical defence investment framework for Wales. This Government is committed to international solidarity, respect for human rights and the rule of international law. We are equally clear that democratic societies have a legitimate right to defend themselves and that the defence, security and resilience sectors play an important role in protecting the freedoms and values that we hold dear.

The world is becoming more uncertain. We are seeing ongoing conflict, including within Europe itself, as well as wider geopolitical instability and increased threats to national security. Wales has a significant aerospace, defence and security sector. The sector supports thousands of highly skilled jobs, sustains important supply chains and contributes to research, innovation and economic growth. Industries such as cyber security, semiconductors, aerospace and advanced manufacturing, autonomous systems and artificial intelligence are all part of the wider economic environment. Welsh businesses and workers should be able to benefit from investment, innovation and growth, including from the defence growth deal.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Welsh Defence Ethical Framework
contributions.text_english:
However, public support for the sector cannot be unconditional. Where the Welsh Government provides support through grants, investment assistance, trade promotion or wider economic development activity, people in Wales rightly expect that support to reflect our values and responsibilities. It's important that we recognise legitimate ethical concerns while supporting a focus on high-quality jobs that the sector sustains in communities across all parts of Wales. It's therefore essential that Welsh Government support is guided by a clear and consistent ethical framework. While decisions on arms exports remain reserved to the UK Government, it is right that the Welsh Government is clear about the principles that guide our own engagement with the sector. We recognise the need for greater clarity in how these decisions are made. That is why we are developing an ethical defence investment framework for Wales.

The purpose of the framework is not to exclude the defence sector from engagement with the Welsh Government, nor to duplicate UK export controls or licensing arrangements. Rather, it is to provide a consistent basis for Welsh Government decision making where devolved support is being considered. In developing the framework, officials are engaging with stakeholders and learning from approaches being taken elsewhere in the UK. The framework will recognise the legitimate role of the defence sector in supporting national security, democratic resilience and economic prosperity, while ensuring Welsh Government decisions are informed by appropriate ethical considerations, including respect for human rights and international humanitarian law.

Our approach will be based on enhanced ethical due diligence. In practice, this means retaining the existing UK legal and regulatory framework while introducing additional ethical considerations to support Welsh Government decision making in the areas mentioned earlier. This will be a proportionate approach designed to provide greater transparency and assurance without creating unnecessary barriers for businesses operating responsibly, legally and in support of our economy and security. The framework will focus on activity taking place in Wales and on the specific projects, products, services or technologies seeking Welsh Government support. This will help ensure that decisions are informed by a clear understanding of the activity being supported, its intended purpose and, where appropriate, its known end users. 

We're also considering the introduction of a proportionate self-declaration process for businesses seeking particular forms of Welsh Government support. This will provide additional transparency and assurance while avoiding unnecessary burdens on businesses operating responsibly and within the law. This framework will also inform Welsh Government participation in defence-related trade missions, exhibitions and business-to-business events, helping ensure a consistent approach across relevant areas of activity. As part of this work, we will also consider how the framework can support innovation and dual-use technologies, recognising that many of the technologies driving economic growth, including cyber, artificial intelligence, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing, have both civilian and defence applications.

Given the significance of this work, and to ensure a consistent approach, I have asked that, where legally and practically possible, any decisions relating to new Welsh Government investment support for defence sector activity are not finalised until the framework is published and implementation arrangements have been fully considered. Should a decision on Welsh Government support be required before publication of the framework, it will be taken by the Prif Weinidog, taking account of relevant considerations. This is a temporary and precautionary measure to ensure that future decisions are considered against the framework from the outset. I want to be clear that this does not represent a withdrawal of support for the sector, nor does it affect existing contractual commitments or the day-to-day relationship between the Welsh Government and defence-related businesses operating in Wales. It does not prevent ongoing engagement, discussions, due diligence or exploratory work with businesses where no investment decision has been taken.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Welsh Defence Ethical Framework
contributions.text_english:
Wales has a proud tradition of championing human rights, international solidarity and the rule of law. We recognise and value the contribution of the workers, businesses, researchers and apprentices across Wales whose skills, expertise and innovation strengthen our security, resilience and economic prosperity. We reject the false choice between ethical responsibility and economic opportunity. At a time of increasing threats to security in Wales and beyond, Wales can support a strong, innovative and responsible defence sector whilst remaining true to the values that define us as a nation. I'm always disappointed when you're disappointed, Janet, and there were so many strands to that, I could be tempted to disappear down a few rabbit holes. Well, I'll give you the answer: it was the UK Conservative Government in 2013. So, look, you can judge us on the framework when it's published, okay. contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Llywydd. I welcome this important debate, and I thank the Member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf for bringing it forward. Think of a 19-year-old young woman in Rhyl who left school three years ago and who hasn't worked since. The research on what happens next is clear. Without support, that young person can carry a wage scar of 10 per cent to 15 per cent, which is still visible at the age of 42, running deeper after each further period spent out of work. In terms of just the economic output, the exclusion of one young person costs about £100,000 over a lifetime to the entire society. In Wales, we estimate that about 50,000 young people aged between 16 and 24 are not in education, employment or training. That is a social failure and an economic failure, too: 50,000 futures narrowed, with the whole of Wales bearing the cost.

We should be precise about who these people are, because the diagnosis determines what the treatment should be. They are not from a single group. Around a third are unemployed in the conventional sense, looking for work but unable to find it. Around two thirds are economically inactive, not looking for work or unable to work. And in this context, illness, and above all mental illness, has become one of the fastest growing drivers. Those who left education the earliest are the most likely to remain disengaged from the labour market the longest. A system built only for jobseekers will continue to miss the larger group. A system built only around health barriers will miss the remainder. And because the routes open or close before a young person reaches the labour market, schools and colleges are part of the solution too. So, we need a comprehensive solution that tackles all of these factors.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
contributions.text_english:
It is right that, at the beginning of this new administration and this new Senedd, we ask some hard questions of the system we've inherited. This Government took office with spending on employability support marginally higher per head than other parts of the UK, and with the proportion of young people who are NEET rising sharply on the most recent survey data. So, higher spending in Wales, yet more young people currently adrift. I don't think anybody in the Siambr would find that acceptable, and the Government doesn't either.

One of the key questions for me is how long after disengaging does the system first reach a young person. Actually, is it the system that's disengaged from them, rather than the young people from the system? I've asked my officials to establish that number precisely. In designing any policy, of course investment matters, but as the Member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf said, outcomes matter more. The measure of success is not the number of job starts or the people on a programme that we can count, but whether a young person is still in good work or learning six months on, and 12 months on. And that's the standard I want applied to every programme in my portfolio.

The young person's guarantee was designed by the previous administration. Governments change but the commitment to young people should not and does not. Under this Government, under this Minister, I want it to grow even stronger. That's why we're proud to support the motion today. No young person in Wales should be left without a route into education, training or work. Our task is not to do less for young people, it's to do better by them, and doing better also demands honesty. Existing policies—UK and Welsh alike—under Governments of every colour have not been sufficient to the task. We need better.

We're not starting from a blank sheet of paper. Some of the most promising results internationally come from approaches that join up employment and health support together, and from guarantees that put a firm time limit on how long a young person waits for an offer. When I meet with Alan Milburn soon, I will discuss these ideas and how we can work as two Governments together. I want to work as a Minister with everyone in this Chamber, and with the cross-party group on youth employment—there's no monopoly on good ideas—and I want our work to be evidence led. I have to say that I haven't seen any convincing evidence myself that immigration is a major contributory factor for youth unemployment.

We do know some things about what works, and we can draw upon the experience of the New Deal for the unemployed, 25 years ago—one of the most successful interventions ever in terms of active labour market policy. We know that tens of thousands of young people are outside work and learning now, while Welsh employers still report vacancies they struggle to fill. What that tells me is that this isn't only about job preparation; it's structural.

It's no good if a job exists but you never hear about it, or you haven't heard about the young person's guarantee, or you can't afford the bus to reach it, or the bus route doesn't even exist to help you get there. Support on its own is not enough because you cannot train a young person into a job that does not exist. So, you need work on the demand side as well as on the supply side. The work of our new development agency in helping to scale Welsh firms, in building the sectors of the future, and in helping some of our traditional sectors like tourism and food and drink to provide those first jobs, is critical. And we will be asking more of employers. To echo the point that was made by one of the Members here, Governments can do so much, but Governments on their own cannot do everything, and in creating first jobs, we need employers to do more as well.

There's a harder challenge that has been on the horizon and has now arrived. Artificial intelligence, on the early evidence, is not abolishing occupations, but it is stripping out the routine tasks from which entry levels were traditionally built in administration, in customer service, in junior professional work. If firms do not redesign the first rung, it will simply disappear. Our responsibility as a Government is to help make sure that technological change expands opportunity rather than narrows it, and we need the skills system to enable us to do that. Our support right across Government must answer the labour market of tomorrow, not the one of 10 or 15 years ago.

None of this works if a young person cannot find the way in. Too often, we ask the young people that are furthest away from the labour market to navigate the most fragmented part of our public services. contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Improving access to local economic opportunities in Casnewydd Islwyn
contributions.text_english:
Dirprwy Lywydd, I would like to thank the Member for Casnewydd Islwyn for bringing this debate before us this afternoon, the final debate of this session, on such an important topic. I'm also grateful for the contributions from other Members. This is a valuable debate, not only about the economic future of one constituency, but about the broader role that the south-east of Wales can play in ensuring prosperity for the whole of Wales. This constituency is unique. In one brief journey, you can go from Caerleon, where the Roman legion dwelt, through Newport, the city of the Chartists, and up the valley, through Risca, Newbridge and Abercarn, to Blackwood—communities that built Welsh industry with their own hands.

There are very few constituencies that capture so much of Welsh history in so few miles, and there are few that hold so much of its future: advanced manufacturing, world-leading innovation, public services that are strong, a skilled workforce, digital industries that are growing, and excellent educational institutions. When we talk about economic growth, it's not the scale of the growth that matters alone; the real question is whether that growth actually increases living standards, creates better paid jobs and strengthens communities. That's why this Government has set an ambitious objective for itself and for Wales to halve the productivity gap between Wales and the UK.

'Productivity' isn't a word that warms the cockles of one's heart, perhaps. As far as I know, nobody's written a poem about it—to date, at least. Perhaps at the next Talwrn y Beirdd, we will see that. But its significance is simple and striking. More productive economies pay higher salaries, they attract more investment and create greater opportunities for future generations. If we are serious about the prosperity of the whole of Wales, particularly in those communities that have too often felt that they have been ignored, then we must tackle Welsh productivity. It's not jargon; it's a salary on a Friday, ultimately, it is sustenance for families and for communities.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Improving access to local economic opportunities in Casnewydd Islwyn
contributions.text_english:
The good news is that Casnewydd Islwyn already holds many of the key ingredients for Wales's economic success. Start with Newport—a city with a habit of arriving early at the future. In 1839, thousands marched down Stow Hill to demand a vote a generation or more before the rest of Britain caught up with them. Newport is early again today. It has become one of Wales's most important economic centres. It is home, as we've heard, to globally significant semiconductor and advanced manufacturing businesses.

The modern world runs on slivers of silicon thinner than a human hair—in our phones, our hospitals, our electric vehicles, in our artificial intelligence—and a remarkable share of that capability globally sits within a few miles of the communities we are discussing this afternoon. Isn't that an exciting thing to say? We were at the heart of an industrial revolution in the past and we are there, right at the centre, at the leading edge today. The growth of the semiconductor cluster in south-east Wales settles an old argument. Wales can compete internationally in high-value, knowledge-intensive industries. Not in theory, but in practice, now. These are precisely the sectors that drive productivity and create the highly skilled, well-paid jobs our communities deserve.

Alongside that industrial strength stands another major asset, the University of South Wales and its Newport campus, of course. A university is not simply a place young people pass through for three years. As an anchor institution, it is part of the economic machinery of the region. Its work in engineering, digital technology, cyber security, business innovation and workforce development helps ensure that local employers can find the skills they need. It provides a vital bridge between research, innovation and commercial opportunity. If Wales is to attract and keep high-value industries, institutions like this one will be central to the mission. The same is true for Coleg Gwent and further education. FE and higher education together, working as a regional version of the team Wales approach, is going to be so central to our economic success.

contributions.item_title_en: 10. Short Debate: Improving access to local economic opportunities in Casnewydd Islwyn
contributions.text_english:
Newport's strengths reach well beyond manufacturing and higher education. This is now the city where the United Kingdom counts itself and registers its ideas. The Office for National Statistics keeps the nation's numbers—this nation, and the one next door, and the one up north as well. The Intellectual Property Office guards its inventions here. There's something quietly satisfying about a city that for too long has been undercounted, I think, in the national story, being the place that does the counting in so many contexts. More practically, perhaps, these organisations have made Newport a hub for highly skilled employment, drawing talented people into the city and creating room for the private sector to grow around them. Add excellent connectivity through the M4 corridor, the rail network, which we are seeking to build out and build upon, and access to wider regional markets, and Newport has become a nexus, a driver of economic activity, not just for itself, but for the wider region and for the nation as a whole.

The same is true of the Valleys communities that give this constituency its unique character. When Victorian engineers wanted to build the tallest railway viaduct in Britain, where did they choose but Crumlin? Blackwood, Newbridge, Risca and Abercarn carry a proud industrial heritage and a workforce with deep experience in engineering, manufacturing and the skilled trades. These communities built the Welsh economy once, but they're not museum pieces; they have an equally important part to play in building the next Welsh economy too.

Now, our challenge is to make sure that investment reaches every part of Wales and every part of this constituency, and, as you've said, that local people can reach the opportunities being created. That means investing in skills, creating, as the Deputy Minister is now doing, and fashioning a skills system that actually delivers the needs of our employers, but crucially as well allows our young people to achieve their true potential, backing local businesses, improving transport, digital connectivity, enabling people to find quality work close to home.

It also means learning from our own history, and few places teach the lesson better than this constituency. For generations, coal came down these valleys to be burned at Uskmouth and exported out of the port, and too much of the wealth it created went elsewhere. For too long, Wales has hosted energy projects without keeping enough of the value they generate. That must now be reversed. If Welsh land, wind, water and sea bed create wealth, the people of Wales should see more of the value of it. The energy story of Casnewydd Islwyn is already turning. At Uskmouth, the old coal-fired power station is being transformed into one of the largest battery storage hubs in the United Kingdom, storing clean power on the very site that once burned Valleys coal. Beside the steelworks at Llanwern sits one of the largest solar developments in Britain. The uplands above the Sirhowy and Ebbw valleys have the wind, and beneath them, the flooded workings of the old collieries hold warm water that mine water schemes elsewhere are already putting into homes. Even our newest industries point the same way, because a semiconductor cluster is a hungry customer for clean, reliable, affordable power. So, the question for this constituency and for Cymru, for Wales as a whole, is no longer whether the energy transition will happen here, it's who will own it, who will drive it and who will benefit from it. That's the question my work on behalf of the Government on a national energy strategy is designed to answer, and we will explore the levers we can use in Wales to build a strategy that benefits the people of Wales and Casnewydd Islwyn economically and socially, to ensure that we maximise that prize.

The strategy will set an ambitious yet reachable energy target, including targets for local community and Welsh public-owned energy. The Basques have done it. Iberdrola, a Basque company, is one of the biggest giants across Europe now, because they designed their manufacturing system, but also their energy system, around ensuring that the benefit was kept. We can do that in Wales as well.

I think crucial to this, of course—. Private development and private capital, in any economy, will always play a central role, and we want to attract that capital to invest in Wales to enable us to achieve our potential, but we cannot do it alone through private development. That's why developing our own public energy company, as I said, but also co-ordinating across the different parts of Government, across the different organisations—that's going to be essential to ensuring that we achieve the potential in Casnewydd Islwyn and across Wales.

That's why the creation of a new national development agency matters so much. On this very point about the confusing landscape that we have at the moment, we want to actually have a single front door. If I am a business owner or an investor or a founder and I want to know where to go, then we need to simplify and streamline that, because we want to work faster and further with those companies to ensure that we maximise the opportunity, not just for them, but for Wales as a whole. Our vision of a development agency reflects our determination to be more ambitious, more strategic, more proactive. It will work to attract inward investment, but crucially as well develop our own businesses to scale up, to strengthen local and regional economies and deliver the high-value jobs that we need.

Crucially, we understand that there's an important role here for transport; it's not a separate issue from economic growth. That's why we're joined at the hip, myself and the Deputy Minister for Transport, because infrastructure is a key part of how we deliver socially and economically for our nation, and for every part of our nation. The south-east Wales regional transport plan gives us a platform to connect communities in Casnewydd Islwyn and across the wider region. We're building further on that plan. We have an ambitious vision in terms of how transport can contribute to ensuring that we have the potential there.

The south Wales metro is central to that ambition still. It must mean better connectivity between trains, buses and exchanges, and between those and people, as they walk, cycle and scoot, making it easier to reach work, training and education, without having to rely on a car for every journey. For the communities of Casnewydd Islwyn, the test is simple: is the investment increasing real access to opportunities across Casnewydd Islwyn, across the wider region in the Valleys and the Cardiff capital region, and across Wales?

Dirprwy Lywydd, the economic story of Casnewydd Islwyn isn't just a story of potential. It's already a place of significant strengths, higher manufacturing capacity that is internationally recognised, with a digital economy and innovation that is developing, major employers in the public sector, a prominent university and communities with a proud history of skills, resilience and enterprise. Those strengths are firm foundations for the future. As we aim towards halving that productivity gap between Wales and the UK, building the industries of the future and establishing a new development agency to encourage growth and investment, constituencies like Casnewydd Islwyn will be at the heart of our success.

And it's no accident that this constituency carries the name of a poet—Islwyn. There is a theme developing here, isn't there? The poet Islwyn from Ynys-ddu in the Sirhowy valley taught us that all is sacred. He was right. There is nothing ordinary about these communities, or the people, or their future, and the work of building that future is already there.

Our aim is clear. The vision is an exciting one. We can take inspiration from the excellence that we see, as I saw when I visited KLA and saw the future of Wales before my very eyes—young people with the highest level of skills, and a company that has laid down roots in broader clusters in a microcosm of the Wales that we want to create. Thank you.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Legislative Consent Motion: Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Bill
contributions.text_english:
Lywydd, diolch yn fawr. I move the motion and recommend that the Senedd gives its consent to the relevant provisions in the Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Bill as set out in the legislative consent memorandum.

Steel is no abstraction to Wales, it is in our bridges and our railways, in the turbines that will power our future and in the history of generations of families from Shotton to Llanwern, from Trostre to Cardiff. contributions.item_title_en: 8. Legislative Consent Motion: Steel Industry (Nationalisation) Bill
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'd like to thank all the Members who contributed to this evening's debate. Let me begin with a concern that is widely shared across the Siambr: the way that this Bill was handled, which did curtail our ability to scrutinise it. The preceding legislation that led to the Scunthorpe operations being effectively put into Government control and then nationalised, of course, was an England-only Bill and it was passed, as I said earlier, in a day. This was a four-nation Bill. It relates not just to a potential move in relation to that one site, but it's a piece of legislation that could be applied to steel operations anywhere in the United Kingdom. Given that, I think the approach should have reflected the devolution settlement.

There was no prior engagement with the Welsh Government. The reason that has been given, I understand, is one of it being commercially confidential. Well, with something that is as strategically important to the future of the Welsh economy and the UK economy, then I don't think that stands up to scrutiny, to be perfectly frank.

We were put in a difficult position, as were the other devolved legislatures. The Northern Ireland Assembly hasn't been able to arrive at a position because there's been simply no time because of the compressed timetable. We, as we always will, will reflect on what we could have done differently, but, in essence, we were put in a very, very difficult position.

What we tried to do was, given that suboptimal position, we tried to get the best result for Wales. Yes, the commitments that we sought in relation to Wales's legitimate interests on behalf of our steel communities—we wanted that in statute, that those are our principles. I think they're principles that will, I think, probably be widely shared right across this Siambr. Now, we were able, because we held out, to get those commitments, at least on the record, and we were successful at least in getting a commitment from the current UK Government. But if they were prepared to make that promise at the despatch box, why weren't they prepared to put it in statute? Because the promise doesn't change, the commitment doesn't change, but, of course, a statutory commitment is always better because you can hold not just this Government to account, but, of course, it stands, then, in the legislation governing future administrations as well, and I simply don't understand the resistance to putting it on a statutory basis.

People have spoken rightly with feeling about Port Talbot, and I will not add further to what I said in opening, except this: we cannot restore what that community lost, but we can make certain that the option to nationalise is firmly available to future Governments if necessary, and that's what consent today achieves, and it's why, in all conscience, we could not do anything other than recommend to the Senedd that we support it. Of course, any policy in relation to nationalisation or wider steel strategy has to be fair, and we have to have fair competition, and I think we were right and other Members are right to raise that. Public ownership exists to rescue an industry, not to distort a market, and if these powers are used in Scunthorpe or anywhere else, we will measure the consequences against the interests of our Welsh steel industry, our Welsh steel companies and communities that depend on that sector, and we'll not stay silent if Wales is made to pay the price of an intervention elsewhere.

But our message today is simple: we consent to this Bill, or we urge the Senedd to do so, because Wales must never again be told that the tools to save our steel do not exist. We consent to this legislation with our eyes open and with our conditions on the record: equal treatment, fair competition and a full Welsh voice whenever these powers touch the interests of our people. Thank you.

Llywydd, next year, that international profile takes on a new dimension. Wales steps on to one of the biggest sporting stages on earth as we welcome hundreds of thousands of Tour de France fans, and there's a certain justice in it—for decades we've been apologising to cyclists for our gradients, and now the greatest race on earth is coming precisely because of them. It turns out we were sitting on a world-class asset all along.

But a great event that leaves nothing behind is just a party. Our ambition is a legacy, so I'm proud to announce today a £4.5 million investment over 2026 and 2027 in tourism-related cycling infrastructure. The peloton will pass through Wales in a matter of hours. What it leaves behind must last for decades. This is about converting a moment of global attention into a permanent national asset—routes, facilities and businesses that serve visitors and communities long after the last rider has crossed the line.

And if we're inviting the world in, the welcome must be real for everyone. A quarter of all visitors to Wales are disabled; if Wales says 'croeso' to the world, that word cannot come with small print. It must hold true for disabled visitors, neurodivergent visitors and people with hidden conditions and barriers. That's why I'm launching Croeso i Bawb, £2 million in grant funding to help tourism and hospitality businesses open their doors wider still. Accessibility is good business, but, more than that, it is simply what 'hospitality' means.

Let me turn now to the two questions at the heart of this debate. Firstly, the visitor levy. Where tourism happens, there are impacts on the local area. That's not a criticism of the sector, it's a facet of success. Visitor levies are neither unusual nor untested. They operate successfully in destinations across Europe and the world, providing resources for the very infrastructure and services that make places worth visiting in the first place. It's, rightly, for each local authority to consult and decide, but, where a levy is introduced, it's an opportunity to make the visitor economy work both for the sector and for the communities that host it, and this Government supports that model.

Second, the 182-day letting threshold. Tourism matters to our economy; so do homes for local people. Those two truths must be held in balance. And where the balance is wrong, we will act. That's why our manifesto committed to reviewing the threshold and creating clear, reasonable exemptions where self-catering accommodation would not qualify as a private home. The Cabinet Minister for Finance is considering these matters as an early priority and will set out our proposals in due course.

Llywydd, the First Minister has said that he is committed to learning at all times, and that will be my approach too. I meet the chairs of the regional tourism forums later this month, and over the summer I'll continue taking evidence directly from sector representatives across Wales, but I do want to go further. Over the course of this term, we are committed to examining whether the form and function of Visit Wales is right for the sector it serves. I believe the moment has come for a proper stocktake, a reset moment between Government and the sector, leading to a shared vision and action plan, a new deal for the visitor economy. I want the sector to help shape it, and I want the Senedd to help shape it too—the cross-party group, Members on all sides, including the parties opposite and the party behind me—for the whole of Wales, built by the whole of Wales. And in that spirit, let me turn now to the contributions Members have made this afternoon.

Anna Nicholl shared some of her constituents' experiences, and I think that, in listening and learning, we need to hold those experiences right at the heart of everything that we do. Steven Rodaway asked us to look at the evidence base, and we certainly will be committed in this and in everything we do to ground everything in the evidence base. We urge Members that want to bring data to our attention to do so, and we will do so ourselves in a transparent manner. I welcome the positive contribution from Shavanah Taj. The levy used well, in partnership with the sector, as we know from across Europe and the world, can actually be an engine of growth and development for the sector. And I know that's the kind of approach that's been taken by the sector in Cardiff. There could be lessons elsewhere in Wales.

I am out of time at this point. The flesh was willing, but the spirit was weak. [Laughter.] All I would say in closing is: look, every nation tells the world a story about itself, and tourism is how the world comes to hear ours. Let's make sure that story is worthy of the country and the country worthy of the welcome.

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: New Development Agency for Wales
contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Dirprwy Lywydd. When I stood in the Siambr to set out our national productivity mission, I committed to updating the Senedd on next steps in establishing a new national development agency for Wales. Less than three weeks into this administration, we announced the most ambitious economic goal in Wales in two decades; namely, halving Wales’s productivity gap with the UK within 10 years. If we are going to achieve that goal, we need a fundamental change in how we approach economic development in Wales. The proposed new agency will be a key driver in achieving that change.

I have a clear vision for the agency: it will improve productivity in Wales, create better jobs for people and put money in their pockets, thereby raising living standards. I want the agency to focus on retaining ownership and economic value in Wales by delivering a clear national focal point for businesses that have the ambition and potential to scale up. I want it to provide support, advice and guidance to help these businesses navigate the finance landscape, strengthening investment readiness and unlocking growth opportunities. Supporting more Welsh-owned firms to grow and scale into resilient, productive and competitive businesses will be crucial. 

We are proud of Wales's strong base of microbusinesses and larger firms, but we have to address the long-standing challenges small to medium-sized businesses face in scaling up. Scaling businesses are those that innovate, that export, that utilise our Welsh skill base and that take advantage of the research and development being driven in our universities. And they're also businesses that can mobilise investor finance to realise their vision. These are innovation-driven enterprises.

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: New Development Agency for Wales
contributions.text_english:
I want the new agency to lead a proactive and highly targeted approach to attracting inward investment into Wales, building on established strengths while sharpening focus and promoting Wales's competitive strengths internationally.

Innovation is central to our economic development strategy and to closing the productivity gap. I see the development agency as a body with innovation at its core. Innovation is so much more than new product development; it ensures the spread, diffusion and adoption of new technology and helps drive economic competitiveness and productivity improvements. Research tells us that much of the growth in productivity comes from innovation and new ideas, rather than simply increasing labour or capital. In simple terms, innovation matters because it helps the economy grow, makes businesses more competitive, and improves people's standard of living over time. 

As set out in our 100-day plan, we're establishing an expert panel to advise us on the design of the new agency. The panel will not operate in isolation; rather, they will engage widely and be outward looking and collaborative in taking forward their work. The panel will be independent of Government and look to international best practice in economic development, as well as tapping into the knowledge and practical experience of businesses in Wales, to make sure their operating environment is fit for the future. We have set out the headline vision. The panel will help us deliver that vision, providing advice, recommendations and challenge about the form and functions of the agency. They will bring their expertise to help us develop the detailed remit and functions of the agency, helping us design and establish an organisation that swiftly supports the growth of the economy. They will provide advice on how the agency can best fit into the wider economic development landscape in Wales, working in collaboration to deliver for our country. And, crucially, they will advise on how the agency can best support productivity improvement, overcoming structural frictions around scaling, to turn opportunities into investable propositions. This new institution must be built on the Wales of today, and of tomorrow, and be able to stand out globally and connect effectively with our businesses across Wales—connecting bro and byd. 

And let me be clear at the outset that the Government is not looking to re-create the previous WDA. I want the new agency to be a more agile and dynamic arm's-length body with innovation at its heart, delivering on the strategic direction set by Welsh Ministers. It will draw on best practice and the best advice from around the world, and, in turn, become an international exemplar in its own right.

Creating a new development agency is a crucial part of driving the positive changes in productivity that we need. But it needs to be a much wider, collective effort across Wales. We need, collectively and collaboratively, to look at the current landscape and work with local and regional partners to create an economic development system where roles are clear and we're all working together as one team for the people of Wales. As part of that team Wales approach, engagement with Members of the Senedd, political parties and social partners such as trade unions is key. Further discussions will take place on the best way to ensure engagement and input over the period the expert panel undertakes its work, and I hope Members across the Chamber will be willing engage positively, collaboratively and creatively with that work.

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: New Development Agency for Wales
contributions.text_english:
The knowledge that we need to inform the design phase of the agency already exists in businesses right across Wales and in the strong connections that Wales has further afield. That's why the advisory panel will be comprised of a core group of individuals with a wealth of business experience. 

I’m pleased today to announce today that Jonathan Lewis, following appointment by the First Minister, will chair the expert advisory panel. Jonathan brings a wealth of business experience and will lead the panel’s deliberations over the coming months. I'm grateful to Jonathan for agreeing to give up his time to provide insight and advice to the Government in this crucial endeavour, and I look forward to working with him. We will now work together to recruit further members of the panel, so that its work can start fully, underpinned by relevant research that is already under way. I will provide a written statement setting out the full membership of the advisory panel in the coming weeks.

Dirprwy Lywydd, the appointment of the chair of the panel to advise on the remit and operating model of the new agency is a key stepping stone in the journey towards making Wales the best place in the United Kingdom to start a business, to grow a business, and to invest in a business. Let the work begin together. I look forward to updating the Senedd on further progress in due course.

contributions.text_english:
I thank the Member for his response. I'd just like to focus a little bit on some of the areas where I think there is common ground between us. In 'Making Wales Work', which was the larger policy document that was the basis for our economic policy set out in the manifesto, we did ourselves, of course, set out the way in which the agency can be a means of ensuring, as we described it, that there is a single front door for business. So, I think we're on the same side and on the same page on that one.

The precise sequencing in terms of when you take different functions into the agency, that's a matter of detail that we're working through. But, absolutely, we want to make sure that businesses have a streamlined level of support. Of course, there will always be the need for specialist support in different areas—finance, as he described, and also exports.

And, by the way, in relation to his last point, we don't just wait for the agency to come along and solve our economic problems. I was speaking to a business last week about an investment project. I'll be doing it again, and I'm doing it all the time—talking to our teams that work in the different areas of business support. So, the existing business support is there, is ongoing. What we're trying to do is to improve the system for the future.

In relation to his point that he made about inward investment, I agree with him. Look, as I set out in my statement, we have to be strategic about inward investment. Foreign direct investment has a role in any economy, but we need to actually focus it on those areas that will be more embedded—through supply chains, as he suggests—in the Welsh economy, that actually build on our existing and possible future strengths. And that is exactly—he's right—what the Irish have done. Through a development agency called the IDA, they have emphasised aftercare, as they call it, because the majority of foreign direct investment is further investment by companies that have already come here. And that's the approach that the IDA have adopted, and it's definitely one that we would want to see at the heart of the strategy of the development agency here.

contributions.text_english:
I'm very grateful to the Member for the spirit of her remarks and the way in which she's engaged as well with me outside of the Siambr. I think these are good questions to ask, and some of them are very much at the core of the process that we're going to go through now. And I do ask Members across the Chamber to engage with that process. Leadership is a combination, you know? It's a combination of having clarity about the goal—and we've set that goal, haven't we? Yes. But also humility to accept that you don't have all the answers. Any politician who says they've got all the answers is misconceived, all right? Some of the best answers will be out there. They will be in the collective intelligence of the nation as a whole. They'll be in people with business experience, some of whom will be involved in this process. They'll be in the trade unions and the social partners. That's why it's important that they have a role here as well.

We want to move at pace. That's one of the clear directions that we will give to the group: that we want to get to a minimal viable proposition in terms of the agency as soon as possible. The agency in year 1 of its operations will look different to the agency in year 4, so let's get there and build the future as fast as we can. 

All I would say in terms of development agencies is that they have played a central role in virtually anywhere that you can think about in the nations and regions that have closed an economic gap. Few of those nations or regions that have had one have got rid of them. We're one of the few exceptions. There may be a reason for that. They are an incredibly valuable tool. Do you need to get the design right? Absolutely. Getting the right relationship in terms of how arm’s length it is from Government but how close it is to a Government is important. It's one of the key questions that we've already done a lot of thinking on, and we will continue as we go through the design process.

I would just urge her and other honourable Members to come with their ideas about how we can get this right for Wales. Because there is a great opportunity here for us to give ourselves an additional lever that we have lacked now for 20 years in order to close the gap, and that's the intention of the Government.

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: New Development Agency for Wales
contributions.text_english: I'm extremely grateful to the Member for that question. Very broadly, we've already identified that the main focus of the agency will be to enable businesses that have the potential to scale up to do that. That means tailored support, identifying the exact barriers facing every business. The position of every business that has the potential to scale up will be different. In some examples, it will mean access to capital; in other contexts, it may need assistance with exports or help with the skills base. Using an account manager approach will ensure that those businesses will receive the support that they need. To respond to one of the points that was made earlier, it's very important that the agency is focused. There was an element of mission creep in the old WDA. So, focusing specifically on supporting the ability of Welsh businesses to scale up is going to be at the heart of this agency's mission.

Because we cannot afford to get this wrong. That is my commitment to the people of Wales. We have to get this right; we cannot get it wrong.

contributions.item_title_en: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: New Development Agency for Wales
contributions.text_english: It's certainly absolutely key that our national productivity mission and closing the productivity gap is translated into real outcomes in terms of people's lives, which is why, as I set out in my statement, this ultimately is about raising living standards. It is about raising the level of wages. It was us, through the co-operation agreement that existed in the previous Senedd, who created the basis for the creation of Ynni Cymru, which helps communities to do exactly what we're talking about here, namely ensuring that they own community energy facilities. We've seen in our past a situation where we had wealth in terms of energy arising from coal but where the benefits were lost, and we don't want to make that mistake again. contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy Priorities
contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much, Llywydd. Wales is open for business. We are a nation with considerable economic strengths. Across our country, we see thriving enterprises, globally competitive industries, strong universities, a highly skilled workforce, and real opportunities in sectors such as advanced manufacturing and clean energy. These are assets that many nations would envy. And yet, for too long, we have not translated those strengths into the level of economic performance we should expect.

It's not a lack of potential that's the central challenge we face, it's a failure to fully realise it. Too often, the different parts of our economic system—investment, infrastructure, academia, skills, export, planning and innovation—have not worked in alignment. When these elements across the private and public sectors connect and reinforce one another, growth follows. And when they do not, opportunity is lost.

That means removing the blockers they face—whether in planning, access to energy, access to finance, or infrastructure. It also means ensuring that the support around them—skills, research and innovation—actively supports their development and growth. This is not about lowering standards, it's about improving how the Government and its partners work, being clearer about priorities and faster in decision making to join up the systems on which businesses depend.

A key challenge we must address is business scale. Too few Welsh businesses grow to the size where they can invest confidently in innovation, make full use of available skills and compete in higher value markets. So, we will focus on supporting firms to grow, to scale up, while strengthening the foundations that enable that growth.

Reform of our skills system is central to this. We will align skills provision more closely with economic need, ensuring it supports higher value activity and enables individuals to move into better paid roles. We will strengthen links between education, employers and research institutions, so that knowledge flows more effectively into the economy.

Alongside this, we will build a stronger innovation system, supporting firms to adopt new technologies, invest in research and development and benefit fully from Wales’s significant research strengths. That's why we will work constructively with the UK Government, aligning policy and investment wherever it is in Wales’s interests to do so.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy Priorities
contributions.text_english:
Well, could I first of all congratulate the Member on his appointment to this important opposition position? I look forward to engaging with him, both in the course of scrutiny in this Chamber, but also more widely as well. There is no monopoly on good ideas, and I think it's important that we engage to the extent that is possible, in a constructive way, to try and collectively help Wales achieve its economic potential.

I'll start with—in that spirit—there were some elements in there where there was common ground, and we're keen to build up the common ground, ultimately. As a nation, this is a collective endeavour. We all have a role to play. Opposition parties—I know; I've occupied that position—also have an important role to play, not only in contributing ideas, but also holding us accountable to the target that we've set.

We agree that creating a business environment that is the most conducive in order to allow businesses to achieve their potential is absolutely essential. We're committed to do that, and we've said we want to hear the ideas of business, principally, because of course they will have the best information about how we can do that. But if the party of the Member from Reform also has practical ideas that we can put into place, short, medium and long-term, then he will find that my door is open.

We're all about building consensus where we can. There was an interesting kind of consensus there between the opposition spokesperson and, indeed, the previous administration, because they both agreed that there was no need for a development agency. I would say: look, we want to be evidence led, and the evidence from right across the world shows pretty conclusively, if you ask pretty much any leading economist in this area, that development agencies are the tried-and-tested tool for any nation, region or anywhere else that has driven up the kind of trajectory in terms of productivity growth that I've described. Is it the only thing that you should do? Absolutely not. We're not going to achieve it just through the development agency, but it's a pretty necessary tool in the toolbox, based on the experience elsewhere.

In terms of the town centres, we absolutely are committed to having a revitalised town-centre strategy for town centres the length and breadth of Wales. They are important in their own right as employers, but they're also critically important in other ways. If we want to attract and retain talent, the quality of place in our communities is absolutely intrinsic in order to achieve that goal as well. So, they are right four-square, front and centre, part of our economic strategy. We will be setting up a town-centre taskforce. We're committed to do that in the first 100 days, and, again, if there are ideas—. I heard a lot of negativity, but if there are positive ideas from the party behind me or anyone else, we are in the business of taking the best ideas that we have, and turning Wales into the best place to set up and grow a business to drive our economic progress along the ambitious but achievable goal that I've set out today.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy Priorities
contributions.text_english:
I welcome the opposition spokesperson, the Labour spokesperson, to her post as well, and I look forward to engaging in detail on all of the issues that she raised. I think that it's important to bring us back, isn't it, to the focus of today, which is the announcement of a goal, a target, which we lacked for 20 years. And one thing that we—. Nobody can absolutely predict the future with 100 per cent certainty. It's not possible, right. But one thing we can predict: if you don't have a goal at all, if you don't have a target at all, you'll never achieve it; you can't even measure progress. And that's why the first step in any plan to revitalise the Welsh economy is to be clear about the direction of travel. In the absence of that clarity in the previous administration, we had decades of drift, didn't we? So, we are setting that right. Actually, I think we've broken all governmental land speed records here. I'm not even three weeks in to being Minister for the economy, and yet we have set out clearly the goal that we are setting for the Welsh economy over the next decade.

And what flows from that then? Many of the things that she's talked about, I agree with. Look, we have to increase the speed of decision making, but part of that comes from aligning your actions, keeping a focus, and you can't do that unless you have a clear goal. Now that we have that, of course, work is already ongoing—many of the elements that she referred to, in terms of the development agency and the role of the development agency. Yes, foreign direct investment will remain, for our economy, as for any economy, an important element within our economic strategy. What it cannot be—. To reference some of the comments from earlier as well, it can't be the only element. It has to be balanced with actually investing in the capability of our own business base, because, of course, they are rooted firms, they are embedded firms, they will actually deliver the platform for long-term growth. But, of course, foreign direct investment can play a part in building up clusters and sectoral competitive advantage, and we will use the development agency to deliver that kind of knowledge and action in a way that will be far more effective than was possible under the previous administration.

We'll have a further opportunity to talk about how the different elements within my portfolio, connectivity, enterprise—. We've made it very clear, of course, that all of these things—economic infrastructure, which includes transport and digital infrastructure, which includes energy as well—all of that needs to be aligned towards this single economic mission goal. If we get that right, if we get the different parts of the system, then, actually, we can really motor. It's important, though, that that energy system delivers for the needs of Wales. We've been here before at other energy revolutions, haven't we, which didn't deliver for Wales. Part of that is about ownership, part of that is understanding what are the energy needs of our communities and our businesses. And yes, that should actually be reflected in competitive advantage for businesses from our energy potential but also, wherever possible, through community ownership actually delivering lower bills for our people as well.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy Priorities
contributions.text_english:
I really welcome the spirit in which the Member has offered her remarks, and I certainly will be taking up her offer of working together, where it is possible, to design solutions to the problems that the people we all represent collectively face in their daily lives, and, in this context, in ensuring that we get the best possible economic outcomes. New ideas from any direction, I think, are absolutely incredibly valuable, and we will approach this important responsibility that we have in a collaborative manner, in the way that she described.

In relation to some of the specifics, the Member is right to point to the absolute centrality of infrastructure. If we think about the productivity goal that we've set out as the mission today, then, you know, most economists would say that there are three key elements in terms of the long-term success of achieving that kind of productivity growth. One is skills, the other one is innovation, the third one is infrastructure, and so getting the infrastructure right so that our businesses then have the platform that they need in order to deliver their own business potential. So, absolutely, we will be focused on that, and you're right to keep us focused on that, and we look forward to further opportunities to explore how exactly we do that.

In relation to the situation in terms of some of the key strategic corridors that she mentioned, one of them has been mentioned several times today, the Menai crossing, and we as a Government are absolutely clear on the importance of that and the resilience of that crossing. We understand absolutely—directly, I think I can say—the urgency of coming up with solutions that are both short-, medium-term and long-term durable ones.

Indeed, just, if I may, Llywydd, to correct the statement that was made earlier about budget agreements, Plaid Cymru actually did agree a budget agreement with the then Labour administration in 2017 for £3 million precisely to support the design and development of a third Menai crossing. To quote Max Boyce, I know because I was there, and that has given us the platform so that we can now, in an accelerated and focused way, move forward.

That work has already started in scoping, and, indeed, we've also had similar conversations in the context of Brynglas as well, and we want to look holistically at the entire network. I can say that the Deputy Minister and I have also had our first expansive discussion about potholes as well. Maintenance is also part of the picture, isn't it, in terms of maintaining our infrastructure. I look forward to continuing this engagement in the manner that she set out, in a constructive way, so we can actually collectively achieve progress on behalf of the people of Wales.

So, I think that the question for us is: can we get smart and creative in using the potential that we have in terms of clean energy in ways that actually deliver lower costs?

We believe that one of the most effective ways of doing that is to build community-owned, locally owned infrastructure. There's proven evidence that that can deliver a lower cost to households. But we'll also be looking at how we can actually use that principle and apply it to businesses as well—so, looking at things like onsite generation, behind the wire, using 'private wire' as in the jargon, which means that you then can avoid some of the network costs that drive up the price. So, we are absolutely keen to have that conversation. Our position on pylons, on new distribution lines, is absolutely clear. Just on cost, building long new lines of distribution over many, many kilometres is not the best way, possibly, to address the cost issue. There are other ways—the ones that I've described—that actually can deliver lower costs for families, for communities and for business, and we'll be focusing creatively and innovatively on those areas where we can have the greatest impact.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy Priorities
contributions.text_english: I really welcome the Member's question and you're right: I think it's long been a shared understanding among those who have looked at the question of why Wales, over many decades, has underperformed compared to its potential that it's this missing middle. We have many micro and small businesses in Wales, which actually are very, very important in terms of our local economy, as we previously described. But what we do lack is those businesses at scale, and getting from small to medium and getting from medium to large, as well, with home-grown businesses, that is a critical element in any country or region that has achieved its economic potential. And so, that will be one of the key areas of focus for the new development agency. And then it's about understanding, 'Look, what are the constraints and what are the opportunities?' They'll be different on a business-to-business basis, and that's why having account managers that are actually then able to tailor that support package—. It might be finance with a particular business. It might be a business that has identified a new export market. Well, that's the kind of very agile, dynamic approach that a development agency can deliver.

contributions.text_english:
I think that's a really great question, and I really look forward, maybe, to having a further conversation with the Member, drawing upon her own evident experience and expertise. I think, how can we get it—? You're absolutely right. We need, actually, if we're going to create the kind of business-facing, agile and dynamic organisation that we need, then we need to draw on business expertise, people that have run, founded and, in some cases, turned around major successful business organisations, both within Wales and internationally. We'll have more to say about this in the next few weeks, but drawing upon that commercial expertise is going to be critical, not just in the design phase that we will be going through, but then in the operational phase as well.

Of course, a public agency always has to have guardrails. There was reference to what went awry in the previous Welsh Development Agency. We understand there needs to be a framework, doesn't there, but also you need to empower and enable an agency to work in a different way than is possible for the centre of Government to do. So, there are some examples that we can draw upon. So, as well as tapping into business acumen and expertise, the other thing we need to do is look around the world, internationally, and say, 'Well, who are the best? Who are the best in class that have really done this?' And then, obviously, translate that into our own context and conditions.

I look forward to engaging with her and with businesses across Wales in order to get this design as right as we can in the early stage, and then make sure that we learn as we go forward, we adapt as we learn more about what works.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy Priorities
contributions.text_english:
I agree. I thank the Member for all those very pertinent questions, actually. We have many of the raw ingredients of success, as I've described, and one of them, actually, is we do have great universities with highly relevant subject-matter expertise. And what we are not so good at—and this is true not just of Wales; it's true of the UK as a whole, actually—we have great ideas, we have great research, but we're not very good at commercialising that research in the way that, for instance, the United States of America, classically, is able to turn knowledge into products for new start-up businesses, some of which grow, of course, significantly to become unicorns. So, there's a bit of bridging work there, and the Government actually plays an important part in providing that bridge.

I think that venture capital, certainly, again, is lacking in the UK. It's certainly lacking in Wales. The Development Bank of Wales, I think, has done a fairly good job at what I would call 'passive capital'—that's business lending, effectively. Venture capital is a form of active capital, where you don't just get money, you actually get the know-how and the knowledge that comes with the money, because those investors really want to protect their investment to the greatest extent possible.

And then, I think we need to look at our start-up ecosystem. Part of building an effective start-up ecosystem comes into where an arm's-length agency is better, because failure and risk are an absolutely necessary part of building a start-up ecosystem. If you only invest in sure-fire bets, then you will never get start-ups that will scale up eventually. You've got to put some guardrails against that where you're involving public money as well. In terms of start-up ecosystems, there are places in the world that do this very well—and I'm not just talking about Silicon Valley; they're in a scale of their own. There are other places similar to Wales that do this well. We will learn from them very quickly indeed. Flanders is one, actually. That's an example of a region that reinvented itself precisely in the manner that I just described.
